source.version: Accepted manuscript for Computers & Education dated March 9th, 2024 (p. 1 box: 'This is an accepted version of a manuscript for publication in Computers & Education ... not the copy of record'); DOI 10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105031. Posted on PsyArXiv (10.31234/osf.io/9z2tc). Not the typeset version of record.
source.title_on_document: ChatGPT Improves Creative Problem-Solving Performance in University Students: An Experimental Study

supplement.where: The document refers to no supplementary material or online appendix. Appendix 1 (evaluation matrix for the Product Improvement Task) is in this PDF, p. 40. The preregistration is at osf.io/q6wtu (p. 9).
supplement.holds: Nothing beyond the main text. All arm means, SDs, t-tests, d values (Table 2, p. 16) and ANCOVA F-tests (pp. 16-17) are in this PDF.

paper_design_summary: University student volunteers were randomly assigned to solve a Product Improvement Task (three ideas to improve a stuffed bunny so Mattel outsells Lego) either with ChatGPT-3.5 open in a second browser tab (n = 77) or without it (n = 68), in a lab. Before that, both groups did an Unusual Uses Task without ChatGPT as a baseline. Two blind experts rated each participant's solutions for quality, elaboration, and originality on 1-5 scales; self-efficacy, self-evaluations, interest, difficulty, and effort were self-reported.

studies.label: Lab experiment: Product Improvement Task with vs. without ChatGPT

assignment.what_was_assigned: Solving the Product Improvement Task with ChatGPT-3.5 (Plus) open in a second browser tab (experimental) vs. without ChatGPT (control).
assignment.quote: Male and female students who volunteered for the experiment were randomly assigned to either the control condition (task resolution without ChatGPT) or the experimental one (task resolution with ChatGPT) prior to the experiment.
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 9: 'The experimental design and research hypotheses were preregistered at Open Science Framework (osf.io/q6wtu).'

arms.name: Experimental (ChatGPT)
arms.description: Solved the PIT with ChatGPT-3.5 (Plus) open in a second browser tab, after a brief description of ChatGPT with example prompts and responses. Separate sessions from the control group.

arms.name: Control (no ChatGPT)
arms.description: Solved the PIT in a browser with no other open tabs and no ChatGPT. Students in both conditions were free to use the browser for other tools, but the paper says no one did.

participants.exclusions: None. 'All the participants passed the attention checks and completed all the required tasks. Therefore, no participants were excluded.' (p. 10). The paper gives group sizes (68 control, 77 experimental; Table 1, p. 11) but no separate count at the moment of assignment; assignment happened 'prior to the experiment', and the paper does not say whether any assigned volunteers failed to attend. Degrees of freedom t(143) and F(1,142) match N = 145.
participants.who: University student volunteers from a pool of approx. 8000 students, receiving a small portion of course credit; mostly social sciences and humanities; 108 BA and 37 MA; mean age about 22.5; 46 male and 99 female (Table 1).
participants.country: Not stated explicitly. The lab was at the first author's institution (Institute of Psychology, Czech Academy of Sciences, Prague, Czech Republic).
participants.quote: The control group for the present study contained 68 university students and the experimental group contained 77 participants
participants.locator: p. 11, Participants and Table 1; p. 9-10, Experimental Procedure

ai_tool.how_used: Second browser tab with ChatGPT open during the PIT. Participants were told ChatGPT responds to prompts, that prompts need detail, and that they could add context or ask it to regenerate responses. The task prompt in the experimental arm began '[With the assistance of ChatGPT,]'. Use was not logged or reported.

task.description: Product Improvement Task adapted from Puente-Díaz et al. (2021): as a Mattel consultant, create three solutions to improve an ordinary 30 cm stuffed bunny that are as original and as useful as possible to help Mattel achieve higher sales than Lego. Preceded by an Unusual Uses Task (paperclip) done without ChatGPT in both arms.
task.duration: Whole experiment: M = 26 (SD = 8) minutes in control, M = 36 (SD = 9) minutes in experimental (p. 10). No time limit stated for the PIT itself.

outcomes.name: PIT quality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two experts (the first and last authors), blind to condition, answers in randomized order, rated quality = extent the answers match the goals (improve the bunny and increase sales), 1 (worst) to 5 (best); weighted kappa = .88 (p. 13; matrix in Appendix 1, p. 40). Preregistered hypothesis H1a. Reported both as an independent-samples t-test and as an ANCOVA with prior ChatGPT experience as covariate.

contrasts.reported: Control M = 2.99 (SD 0.86, N = 68) vs Experimental M = 3.60 (SD 0.89, N = 77); t(143) = 4.16, p < .001, d = 0.69. ANCOVA (covariate: prior ChatGPT experience): F(1,142) = 19.07, p < .001, partial eta squared = .12.
contrasts.locator: p. 16, Table 2 row 4 and H1 text; Ns from p. 11, Table 1

outcomes.name: PIT elaboration
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same two blind experts; elaboration = amount of detail, 1-5; weighted kappa = .93 (p. 13; Appendix 1, p. 40). Preregistered hypothesis H1b.

contrasts.reported: Control M = 2.21 (SD 0.74, N = 68) vs Experimental M = 2.79 (SD 1.11, N = 77); t(143) = 3.65, p < .001, d = 0.61. ANCOVA: F(1,142) = 14.87, p = <.001, partial eta squared = .10.
contrasts.locator: p. 16, Table 2 row 5 and H1 text; Ns from p. 11, Table 1

outcomes.name: PIT originality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same two blind experts; originality = uniqueness of the ideas, 1-5; weighted kappa = .85 (p. 13; Appendix 1, p. 40). Preregistered hypothesis H1c. Robustness variant: mixed ANOVA on z-scored originality, UUT (pre-test, no ChatGPT) vs PIT, group x task interaction F(1,142) = 7.79, p = .006, partial eta squared = .05 (p. 17, Figure 1).

contrasts.reported: Control M = 2.21 (SD 0.91, N = 68) vs Experimental M = 2.74 (SD 1.02, N = 77); t(143) = 3.32, p < .001, d = 0.55. ANCOVA: F(1,142) = 12.56, p < .001, partial eta squared = .08. Baseline-by-task interaction (z-scores): F(1,142) = 7.79, p = .006, partial eta squared = .05; Figure 1 shows z-score means with 95% CI error bars only graphically.
contrasts.locator: p. 16, Table 2 row 6 and H1 text; p. 17, Figure 1 and text; Ns from p. 11, Table 1

outcomes.name: Unusual Uses Task originality (baseline, before ChatGPT exposure)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Paperclip Unusual Uses Task done without ChatGPT in both arms before the PIT and before the experimental arm saw the ChatGPT description; originality rated 1-5 by the same two blind experts, weighted kappa = .80, mean of both (p. 12). It is a post-assignment, pre-exposure baseline (balance check), so it answers none of the three questions; listed for completeness.

contrasts.reported: Control M = 1.74 (SD 0.99) vs Experimental M = 1.71 (SD 0.81); t(143) = 0.18, p = .855, d = 0.03. Pre-test difference: F(1,142) = 0.01, p = .928, partial eta squared = .00.
contrasts.locator: p. 16, Table 2 row 1; p. 17, text below Figure 1

company_involvement.description: No company involvement, funding statement, or conflict-of-interest statement appears in this accepted manuscript. The task scenario names Mattel and Lego, but neither took part.

eligibility.reason: Individuals were randomly assigned to solve an idea-generation task with or without ChatGPT (p. 10); 145 students analyzed, 77 vs 68, no exclusions (pp. 10-11); blind expert ratings of quality, elaboration, and originality of the solutions (pp. 12-13, Table 2 p. 16).

one_line_finding: Students with ChatGPT produced product-improvement ideas rated higher by blind experts on quality (3.60 vs 2.99, d = 0.69), elaboration (2.79 vs 2.21, d = 0.61), and originality (2.74 vs 2.21, d = 0.55) than students without it (Table 2, p. 16).
open_questions: Control and experimental groups had separate sessions (p. 10: 'The control group and experimental groups had separate sessions'), so session is confounded with condition; the paper does not say how sessions were scheduled.
The paper gives no count at assignment; whether any randomized volunteers did not attend is not stated, so n_randomized is left null.
No outcome is named primary; quality, elaboration, and originality are the three parts of preregistered hypothesis H1 (H1a-c). The preregistration (osf.io/q6wtu) was not checked.
notes: Outcomes not listed because they are self-reports, not scored on the output: self-efficacy without/with ChatGPT (Table 2 rows 2-3), self-evaluation of quality and originality (rows 7-8), interest, difficulty, effort (rows 11-13), and perceived usefulness of ChatGPT (row 14). The bias indices (rows 9-10) combine self-evaluation with expert-rated performance and measure metacognitive accuracy, not creativity (Bias quality 0.04 vs 0.02, p = .694; Bias originality 0.14 vs 0.09, p = .371). The raters are two of the authors (first and last). Ratings appear to be one score per participant's full response (three solutions), consistent with t(143). Table 3 (p. 18) gives within-arm correlations only. Both arms could use the browser for other tools, but the paper says no one did (p. 10). The experimental arm spent about 10 more minutes on the whole experiment (p. 10).
